Changes in thermal diffusivity stem from changes across all three of the component parameters as defined in Equation 2: thermal conductivity (k), specific heat capacity (c ), and p density (ρ). In this study, there was no significant attempt made to decouple the component properties from the measured data, though, some comparisons to high temperature solid-phase data are presented. k α≡ (2) ρ·c p Thermal diffusivity inherits crystal structure sensitivity from its underlying parameters, therefore, it is most pertinent to discuss only the (UMo) gamma phase. Although there may be deviations from a BCC linear mixture in some instances, the density and the specific heat of a single phase tends to increase or decrease monotonically between terminal properties (Tritt 2004). Thermal conductivity is driven by electrical and phonon scattering properties, and since uranium and molybdenum are both conductive metals, the electrical scattering tends to dominate. Therefore, since the thermal conductivity increases with temperature for pure uranium, the same would be expected for a single composition of a U-rich alloy. Alloying of materials tends to increase the number of scattering centers, thereby lowering the thermal conductivity given no change in crystal structure. Therefore, the general expectation is that there would tend to be a minimum in conductivity near the point at which there is maximum alloying. Driven by these generalities, it is expected that the thermal diffusivity overall would initially decrease with added Mo content before increasing toward the pure Mo value. Indeed, the temperature and composition specific data collected for this study that are presented in Table 4 and shown graphically in Figure 6 exhibit the expected trends described above. Overall, there was some difference between the measured values during heating and cooling, indicating either some influence of partially transformed crystal structure(s) or a microsegregation effect. The reported values are the average between heating and cooling and no significant effort was made to determine the cause of the difference since it was relatively minor. The behavior of the high temperature gamma phase as a function of composition and temperature is less well developed currently and the best information available is an interpolation of behavior.
